title: Quiz: GLMs — Logistic and Poisson Regression

questions.text: In a logistic regression, the logit link maps P(Y=1) to the linear predictor. What does 'inverting' the link function give you?
options: The predicted probability P(Y=1) = 1 / (1 + e^(−η)), which is always in (0,1)
The odds ratio for each predictor
questions.explanation: The logit link is g(μ) = log(μ/(1−μ)) = η. Inverting gives μ = P(Y=1) = eη/(1+eη) = 1/(1+e^(−η)). This is the logistic sigmoid function, which always maps any real η to a value in (0,1) — solving the problem of OLS predicting probabilities outside [0,1].

questions.text: In logistic regression, exp(β₁) is the odds ratio: it tells you by what factor the odds of the event change for a one-unit increase in x₁.
questions.explanation: The log-odds model is log(odds) = β₀ + β₁x₁. A one-unit increase in x₁ changes the log-odds by β₁, which multiplies the odds by exp(β₁). This is the odds ratio (OR). OR > 1 means x₁ increases the odds; OR < 1 means it decreases them.

questions.text: In Poisson regression with glm(y ~ x, family = poisson()), the coefficient for x is β₁ = 0.03. How do you interpret exp(β₁)?
options: Each unit increase in x adds 0.03 to the expected count
Each unit increase in x multiplies the expected count by exp(0.03) ≈ 1.030 — a 3% increase in the rate
The expected count is 3% of x
The model explains 3% of the variance in counts
questions.explanation: In Poisson regression with the log link, the model is log(μ) = β₀ + β₁x, so μ = exp(β₀ + β₁x). A unit increase in x changes μ by a factor of exp(β₁) — this is the rate ratio. exp(0.03) ≈ 1.030 means a 3% increase in the expected count per unit increase in x.

questions.text: You fit a logistic model for P(dep_delay > 30) and get AIC = 189,000. The null model (intercept only) has AIC = 191,000. What can you conclude?
options: The predictors explain more than 50% of the variance in departure delays
The model with predictors is preferred (ΔAIC = 2,000 >> 10), but the absolute AIC values suggest the predictors explain only a modest fraction of delay risk
The null model is preferred because it is simpler
AIC cannot be used for logistic regression
questions.explanation: ΔAIC = 2,000 is overwhelming evidence for the model with predictors. However, a logistic model AIC of 189,000 on 336,776 observations suggests the model has modest predictive power overall — AIC measures relative goodness of fit, not absolute. The large ΔAIC just means the predictors are statistically useful, not that they explain most of the variation.

questions.text: Which R function fits a Poisson regression for count data?
questions.explanation: Poisson regression is a GLM fitted with glm(). The family = poisson() argument specifies the Poisson distribution with the canonical log link. lm() only handles the normal (Gaussian) family. nlm() is a general numerical minimiser, not a GLM function.

questions.text: The deviance D = −2log(L̂) in a GLM plays the same role as RSS in an OLS model — it measures lack of fit.
questions.explanation: Deviance is the GLM generalisation of RSS. For normal errors, deviance = RSS/σ². For binomial and Poisson, deviance measures how far the fitted model is from the saturated model (which perfectly fits the data). Residual deviance / residual df ≈ 1 indicates good fit; >> 1 indicates overdispersion.
